chapters.title: Pharisees, Sadducees, Essenes and Others
chapters.subtitle: Who was who in the Jewish world of Jesus
chapters.nutshell: First-century Judaism was not one single block. It had several schools and groups that argued about Scripture, purity, the Temple and Rome. Knowing who they were helps you hear the Gospel debates as a family conversation, not as 'Jesus versus the Jews'.
chapters.bigIdea: Jesus stood inside a lively Jewish world of many voices, and His sharpest debates were with people who shared His love for the Torah.
skeleton: Judaism in Jesus' day had many groups, all loyal to the one God and the Torah
Pharisees taught the people; Sadducees ran the Temple
Essenes withdrew to live in strict purity; revolutionaries wanted to fight Rome
Around them stood priests, scribes, Samaritans, ordinary people and Gentile God-fearers
The synagogue was the meeting place where Scripture was read and explained
Jesus' debates are an argument inside the family

p: When we read the Gospels, it is easy to imagine 'the Jews' as one group with one opinion. In fact, the Jewish historian **Josephus** (late first century) describes several 'schools of thought': Pharisees, Sadducees and Essenes, plus a 'fourth philosophy' of rebels against Rome (*Antiquities* 18.11–25). All of them worshipped the one God, kept the Sabbath and honoured the Torah. They disagreed about how to live it out.

The **Pharisees** were respected teachers among ordinary people. They held to the written Torah and also to the 'tradition of the elders' (Mark 7:3), and they believed in the resurrection and angels (Acts 23:8). Paul was a Pharisee (Philippians 3:5), and so were Nicodemus and Gamaliel (John 3:1; Acts 5:34).

The **Sadducees** were mostly wealthy priestly families linked to the Temple. They rejected the Pharisees' oral traditions and denied the resurrection (Mark 12:18). Because they held power, they usually worked with Rome to keep order. After the Temple fell in AD 70, they disappeared.

The **Essenes** lived by strict rules of purity and shared property. Many scholars link them with the community at **Qumran**, near the Dead Sea, where the **Dead Sea Scrolls** were found from 1947 onward — though this link is still discussed. They believed the Jerusalem priesthood was corrupt. The New Testament never names them.

Others wanted to throw off Rome by force, like Judas the Galilean (Acts 5:37). A party called the **Zealots** appears clearly during the war of AD 66–70; Simon 'the Zealot' (Luke 6:15) may have been a rebel or simply 'zealous'. The **Herodians** (Mark 3:6; 12:13) were supporters of Herod's family.

**Priests** and **Levites** served in the Temple by turns (Luke 1:8; 10:31–32). **Scribes** were experts in the Law who copied, taught and applied it; many were Pharisees (Mark 2:16). The **Samaritans** worshipped on Mount Gerizim and accepted only the five books of Moses (John 4:20).

Most people were farmers, fishers and workers. Later rabbis called less strict common folk *am ha-aretz*, 'people of the land' (compare John 7:49). **Tax collectors and 'sinners'** were seen as outsiders (Mark 2:15–16). Some Gentiles, called **God-fearers**, joined synagogue worship without becoming Jews, like Cornelius (Acts 10:2).

sections.h: The synagogue: the village meeting place
p: Every town had a **synagogue** (Greek for 'gathering'). On the Sabbath people prayed, read the Torah and the Prophets, and heard an explanation (Luke 4:16–21; Acts 15:21). A local leader ran it, like Jairus (Mark 5:22). Jesus taught in synagogues across Galilee, and Paul began in synagogues in every city.

> Jesus said: 'The scribes and the Pharisees sit on Moses' seat, so do and observe whatever they tell you, but not the works they do' (Matthew 23:2–3). He respected their teaching while criticising hypocrisy.

Jesus agreed with the Pharisees on the resurrection and on many points of the Law, and some Pharisees warned Him of danger (Luke 13:31). His strong words are like a prophet speaking to his own people. Later Jewish writings also criticise hypocritical Pharisees. Reading the Gospels as a family debate keeps us from turning them into an excuse for contempt.

chapters.title: The Temple: Heart of Jewish Life
chapters.subtitle: The house of God where heaven and earth met
chapters.nutshell: For Jews in Jesus' day, the Temple in Jerusalem was the place where God's presence dwelt among His people. Its courts, priests, daily offerings and festivals shaped the whole year. Many Gospel scenes happen there, and its destruction in AD 70 changed Jewish and Christian faith forever.
chapters.bigIdea: The Temple was the meeting place of God and Israel, and the New Testament presents Jesus and His people as the place where God now dwells.
skeleton: Herod rebuilt the Second Temple on a huge scale
Its courts moved step by step closer to God's presence
Priests served in turns, offering sacrifices morning and afternoon
Pilgrims came for the great feasts and paid the Temple tax
Jesus taught, cleansed and spoke about the Temple; the veil tore at His death
The Temple fell in AD 70, and faith had to find its centre anew

p: The Temple of Jesus' day was the **Second Temple**, first rebuilt after the exile (Ezra 6:15). About 20/19 BC, **Herod the Great** began a huge rebuilding. Work went on for decades — 'it has taken forty-six years to build this temple' (John 2:20). The platform still stands in Jerusalem; its western retaining wall is today called the Western Wall.

sections.h: Courts: closer and closer to God
p: The Temple was built in rings of holiness. Anyone could enter the large **Court of the Gentiles**. A low barrier (the *soreg*) carried warning signs in Greek: no foreigner may pass, on pain of death. Two of these stone inscriptions have been found. Paul was accused of bringing a Gentile past it (Acts 21:28–29).

Inside lay the **Court of the Women**, with the offering boxes where the poor widow gave two coins (Mark 12:41–44); then the **Court of Israel**, the **Court of the Priests** with the great altar, the **Holy Place** with the lampstand, and finally the **Holy of Holies**, entered only by the high priest on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16).

Priests were divided into **24 courses** (1 Chronicles 24), each serving a week at a time. Zechariah, John the Baptist's father, was chosen by lot to offer incense while the people prayed outside (Luke 1:8–10).

Every day a lamb was offered in the morning and another in the afternoon — the **Tamid**, 'continual' offering (Exodus 29:38–42). These became the hours of prayer: 'Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer, the ninth hour' (Acts 3:1), about 3 pm.

Three times a year Israel went up for **Passover, Shavuot and Sukkot** (Deuteronomy 16:16); Jesus' family went every Passover (Luke 2:41). Each Jewish man paid a yearly **half-shekel** Temple tax (Exodus 30:13; Matthew 17:24–27).

Pilgrims needed approved coins and animals for sacrifice, so traders and **money changers** worked in the outer court. Jesus overturned their tables, quoting Isaiah 56:7, 'My house shall be called a house of prayer for all the nations', and Jeremiah 7:11 (Mark 11:15–17).

Jesus was presented there as a baby (Luke 2:22), taught in its courts, and called it 'my Father's house' (Luke 2:49). He also warned that not one stone would remain on another (Mark 13:2). When He died, 'the curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom' (Mark 15:38). Hebrews sees this as a new way into God's presence (Hebrews 10:19–20).

In AD 70 Roman armies under Titus burned the Temple. Jewish tradition remembers this on the fast of **Tisha B'Av**. Without sacrifices, Jewish teachers taught that prayer, Torah study and deeds of loving-kindness carry on the Temple's work, citing Hosea 6:6, 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice'.
> The New Testament speaks of Jesus' body as the Temple (John 2:19–21) and of His people as 'God's temple' where the Spirit dwells (1 Corinthians 3:16).

chapters.title: The Jewish Year: Sabbath and Feasts
chapters.subtitle: The rhythm of time that Jesus lived by
chapters.nutshell: Jesus lived by a Jewish calendar of weekly Sabbaths and yearly feasts. Each feast retold part of Israel's story with God. The Gospels often place Jesus' words and deeds at these feasts, so knowing them unlocks their meaning.
chapters.bigIdea: The Sabbath and the feasts were Israel's way of remembering God's saving acts, and the New Testament shows Jesus filling them with new meaning.
skeleton: The Jewish year follows the moon and the harvests
The Sabbath is the weekly gift of rest
Spring feasts remember the Exodus and the first harvest
Autumn feasts call for repentance, atonement and joy
Later feasts, Hanukkah and Purim, remember rescue
Jesus' life is woven through these feasts

sections.h: A calendar of moon and harvest
p: The Jewish month begins with the new moon, and a month is added in some years so the feasts stay in their seasons. The year of feasts begins in spring with **Nisan** (Exodus 12:2), while the new year is celebrated in autumn in **Tishrei**. Leviticus 23 lists the 'appointed times' of the LORD. Three of them were **pilgrim feasts**, when people went up to Jerusalem (Deuteronomy 16:16), singing the Psalms of Ascents (Psalms 120–134).

The **Sabbath** runs from Friday sunset to Saturday sunset. It remembers creation (Exodus 20:8–11) and freedom from slavery (Deuteronomy 5:12–15). It is not a burden but a gift and a delight (Isaiah 58:13).

Jesus went to the synagogue on the Sabbath 'as was his custom' (Luke 4:16). His Sabbath debates were about how to keep it, not whether to: 'The Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath' (Mark 2:27). Healing on the Sabbath showed its purpose — rest and restoration.

**Passover** (Nisan 14) remembers the lamb's blood and Israel's escape from Egypt (Exodus 12). It flows into the seven days of **Unleavened Bread**. **Firstfruits** offered the first sheaf of barley; Paul calls the risen Jesus 'the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep' (1 Corinthians 15:20).

Fifty days later came **Shavuot** ('Weeks'), called **Pentecost** in Greek. It celebrated the wheat harvest, and Jewish tradition later linked it with the giving of the Torah at Sinai. On this feast the Spirit came on the disciples (Acts 2).

The **Feast of Trumpets** (Tishrei 1, today Rosh Hashanah) begins ten days of soul-searching. Then comes **Yom Kippur**, the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16), a day of fasting, confession and cleansing.

Five days later, **Sukkot** (Tabernacles) is the most joyful feast: families live in booths for a week. The Mishnah describes priests pouring water at the altar and giant lamps lighting the Temple courts (Sukkah 4–5). At this feast Jesus cried, 'If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink' (John 7:37–39) and 'I am the light of the world' (John 8:12).

**Hanukkah** (Kislev 25) remembers the Maccabees cleansing and rededicating the Temple in 164 BC (1 Maccabees 4:52–59). John mentions it: 'It was the Feast of Dedication at Jerusalem. It was winter' (John 10:22). **Purim** (Adar 14) celebrates the rescue of the Jews in the book of Esther (Esther 9).

The Last Supper took place at Passover time. Matthew, Mark and Luke present it as a Passover meal, while John places Jesus' death as the lambs were prepared (John 19:14); scholars still discuss how to fit these together.

> The oldest written description of the Passover meal (Mishnah Pesachim 10) is from about AD 200, so we should not assume every later custom was already in place. Still, the cups, the bread, the story and the hymns echo through the Gospel accounts.

chapters.title: The Herods: A Family in the Gospels
chapters.subtitle: One family, many rulers, from Bethlehem to Paul's trial
chapters.nutshell: Several different men called 'Herod' appear in the New Testament. They belong to one ruling family that served Rome for over a century. Knowing who is who makes many stories in the Gospels and Acts much clearer.
chapters.bigIdea: The Herods held power by building great cities and pleasing Rome, while the true King came as a child they could not destroy.
skeleton: Herod the Great ruled the whole land as Rome's client king
After his death his kingdom was divided among three sons
Antipas ruled Galilee in the time of John the Baptist and Jesus
His grandson Agrippa I persecuted the church
Agrippa II heard Paul's defence
Their power faded as God's kingdom spread

p: Herod came from an Idumean family that had become Jewish. Rome named him 'King of the Jews' in 40 BC, and he took Jerusalem in 37 BC. He was a brilliant builder — the Temple, the port of **Caesarea**, and fortress-palaces at **Masada**, **Herodium** and **Machaerus**. He was also fearful and cruel: he executed his wife Mariamne and three of his sons.
This is the Herod of Matthew 2, who tried to kill the child born in Bethlehem. He died in 4 BC (the most common dating) and was buried at Herodium, where his tomb was identified in 2007.

Rome divided Herod's land between three sons. **Archelaus** ruled Judea and Samaria so harshly that Joseph avoided him and settled in Nazareth (Matthew 2:22–23); Rome removed him in AD 6 and put Judea under Roman governors, later including Pilate.
**Philip** ruled the northeast quietly and rebuilt Caesarea Philippi, where Peter confessed Jesus as the Messiah (Matthew 16:13–16). **Herod Antipas** received Galilee and Perea.

Antipas is 'Herod the tetrarch' of the Gospels. He rebuilt **Sepphoris**, near Nazareth, and founded **Tiberias** on the Sea of Galilee. He married **Herodias**, his brother's wife, and John the Baptist condemned it (Mark 6:17–18). Herodias's daughter danced, and John was beheaded; Josephus says this happened at Machaerus.
Jesus called Antipas 'that fox' (Luke 13:32). During Jesus' trial Pilate sent Him to Antipas, who mocked Him (Luke 23:7–12). Rome exiled Antipas in AD 39.

**Agrippa I**, a grandson of Herod the Great, briefly ruled almost all of his grandfather's kingdom (AD 41–44). He killed James the brother of John and imprisoned Peter, then died suddenly at Caesarea (Acts 12). Josephus also describes his sudden death there.

His son **Agrippa II**, with his sister **Bernice**, heard Paul's defence at Caesarea. Agrippa said, 'In a short time would you persuade me to be a Christian?' (Acts 26:28). Another sister, Drusilla, was married to the governor Felix (Acts 24:24).
> The Herods built palaces, ports and fortresses, but their rule depended on Rome and often on fear. The Gospels set beside them a King born in a village, who was mocked by Antipas yet raised by God.
Their story also helps us read the Gospels carefully: when you see the name 'Herod', ask which one — the father, the son, or the grandson.
